title: Maghi at Muktsar
hook: the fair at Muktsar in January remembers the Forty Liberated

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hola Mohalla: horses, gatka and poetry the day after Holi. Your line was strength, in joy. Did your body get to do something glad? Day one hundred fifty-three.

Most of us know someone who walked away and then came back. The friend who went quiet for a year and finally texted: sorry. The brother who left home angry and turned up one Thanksgiving. Maybe it was you. Coming back is hard, because you have to walk in past everything you said on the way out. Every January, in a town in Punjab called Sri Muktsar Sahib, a huge fair fills the streets, and at its heart is a story about forty men who did exactly that.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO WENT QUIET.` → `WALKING BACK IN.` → `FORTY MEN WHO CAME BACK.`

segments.voice: The fair is called Maghi, because it falls on the first day of Magh, a winter month in the Punjabi calendar, usually in mid-January. The story goes back to the early 1700s. Guru Gobind Singh and his Sikhs had been under siege at Anandpur for months, and food had run out. Tradition says a group of about forty Sikhs from the Majha region decided they'd had enough. The Guru let them go, but asked them to put it in writing: a note saying, in effect, you are not our Guru, and we are not your Sikhs. They signed it and went home. At home they weren't welcomed as heroes. Tradition remembers a woman, Mai Bhago, also called Mata Bhag Kaur, who shamed them for leaving, and then rode back with them herself. They caught up with the Guru's small band near a lake called Khidrana, just as Mughal troops closed in. The forty stood and fought, and they fell. Afterward, the Guru walked among the fallen. One of them, Mahan Singh, was still barely alive. He asked for one thing: tear up the note. Tradition says the Guru took it from his clothes, tore it in front of him, and Mahan Singh died at peace. The Guru called them the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated, and the place became Muktsar, the pool of liberation. Look at what the story honors. Not people who never left. People who left, and came back anyway. And a Guru who had kept the note close all along, so it could be torn.
screen: `MAGHI — THE FIRST DAY OF MAGH.` · `FORTY SIGN A NOTE AND LEAVE.` · `MAI BHAGO LEADS THEM BACK.` · `THE NOTE, TORN UP.` · then, large: `CHALI MUKTE — THE FORTY LIBERATED.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and think of someone who came back. A friend who returned after a silence. A relative who made it home. Someone who came back to health, or to sobriety, or to their faith, or to you. Picture their face at the moment they walked back in, and notice what it cost them. Now, if you're willing, think of one place you left that you might one day return to. You don't have to go. Just look at the door. If you pray, you can hold both of them in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Maghi. The first day of the winter month of Magh, when the fair at Muktsar remembers the Forty Liberated.

Your line: come back, anyway. Today, send one small message to someone you drifted away from. Two words is plenty. Or, if someone comes back to you, let them in without the speech. Day one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: On Maghi, in mid-January, Sikhs gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib for a large fair, bathe in the sacred pool, and remember the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated, with kirtan, prayers and langar.

original.note: Gurmukhi: of Magh, the winter month; the day of the Muktsar fair.

trapdoor: what you thought: a winter fair.
what it means: the first day of Magh, when Sikhs remember forty who left the Guru and came back to die for him.
what a scholar hears: Muktsar is mukt, liberated, plus sar, pool; the old name was Khidrana, and the note is remembered as the bedava, a disclaimer.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 5, life of Guru Gobind Singh (Khidrana / Muktsar)

notes: The battle of Khidrana is usually dated to late 1705; its relation to the Maghi date is debated. The script says only 'the early 1700s'. Confirm.

Mai Bhago's alternative name Mata Bhag Kaur: confirm.
